validity.notes: Existence is strongly corroborated: this is an active, currently-regulated NYSEG gas transmission facility, not a stale or phantom record. Independent sources: (1) NY DPS/PSC docket Case 19-E-0378 et al. (documents.dps.ny.gov, Exhibit JP-KS series, filed 2020) contains extensive NYSEG-authored interrogatory responses discussing the DeRuyter pipeline in granular operational detail (customer counts, compressor station, gate stations, PHMSA reporting); (2) AllOtsego.com news article quoting NYSEG's own March 2019 PSC filing describing DeRuyter mains directly; (3) The Daily Star (Oneonta, NY) guest commentary (2019) discussing NYSEG's DeRuyter replacement/expansion plans. No indication this pipeline does not exist or has been retired.

No duplicate found. GGIT snapshot search for 'DeRuyter' in PipelineName/OtherEnglishNames returns only P0310 (this row, Status=operating) and P1926 (a separate 'Expansion' project, Status=cancelled/shelved). P1926 is a legitimately distinct project phase (the larger 50-mile/12-inch expansion proposal debated in the Daily Star commentary and ultimately not built as originally scoped) and is not in this batch's roster. P0310 is not a double-count.

Considered and not flagged as a concern, but worth recording: the NY PSC docket describes DeRuyter as a 'mid-size branch pipeline' serving ~9,200 end customers directly, which could read as distribution-like. However, NYSEG's own PSC filing (quoted in AllOtsego) explicitly calls the mains 'gas transmission gas mains,' and the PHMSA annual-report attachment in the same docket exhibit is filed under the federal Natural Gas TRANSMISSION and Gathering Systems form (49 CFR Part 191/192), not the distribution form. Federal PHMSA classification is treated as authoritative here. PipelineType=transmission (as currently implied by inclusion in GGIT) is not contested. Caveat: the PHMSA attachment embedded in the docket (Exhibit KS-4, Att. 1, 'ANNUAL REPORT FOR CALENDAR YEAR 2018 NATURAL OR OTHER GAS TRANSMISSION and GATHERING SYSTEMS,' filer = New York State Electric & Gas Corp, OPID-level) is NYSEG's COMPANY-WIDE transmission report (Part J total = 20.34 miles across all NYSEG transmission-classified pipe), not a DeRuyter-only filing — its Part H (miles-by-NPS) and Part J (miles-by-decade) tables were NOT used as DeRuyter-specific corroboration for Diameter/Length/ConstructionYear per the rule that a system/aggregate figure is never a valid ref for a segment-level cell.

GEM's current LengthKnown=40.2km (25 miles) appears to reflect only the FIRST-PHASE/partial replacement scope, not the full DeRuyter mains network. Two NYSEG-originated documents in the same PSC rate case (Case 19-E-0378 et al.) both point to a ~50-mile total: (1) AllOtsego.com (allotsego.com/how-to-waste-400-million/) directly quotes NYSEG's March 15, 2019 PSC filing: NYSEG 'will replace approximately 50 miles of 8-inch and 10-inch 298 psig-coated steel gas transmission gas mains...' (future tense — describing existing mains slated for replacement); (2) the NY DPS docket interrogatory response NYRC-0878 (KS-5, July 2019) states that NYSEG's earlier 2015/2016-era cost estimate 'would involve replacement of an 8-inch section of pipeline between Norwich and Oneonta with a 10-inch pipe, for a total of approximately 25 miles' — i.e. only about HALF of the full network — consistent with a ~50-mile total. Candidate replacement value: LengthKnown ~80.5 km (~50 miles), LengthKnownUnits=km. Tier=medium: both documents originate from the same NYSEG filer in the same rate case (not fully independent origins), though they are two textually distinct filings (a PSC rate filing vs. a discovery-response quoting an internal 2016-2020 Capital Investment Plan) rather than one document repeated. A third source (Daily Star guest commentary, 2019) also discusses '25 miles' vs. a rival '50 miles of 12-inch' EXPANSION alternative, but that passage concerns the proposed NEW/bigger pipe option (a different scope than the existing-mains total) and was NOT used as corroboration here to avoid conflating replacement-project scope with base-infrastructure length. Recommend a human research follow-up to confirm whether 40.2km/25mi or ~80.5km/50mi is the more defensible LengthKnown; not force-applied as an automatic overwrite given the tier.

GEM's current Capacity=1.45 bcm/y is not sourced (MISSING_REF) and appears to be materially overstated relative to the one capacity figure found in NYSEG's own records. The NY DPS docket (interrogatory response NYRC-0878/KS-5) quotes NYSEG's 2016-2020 five-year Capital Investment Plan verbatim: 'The DeRuyter transmission mains were installed in 1953 and lack sufficient capacity to supply the Winney Hill 1st stage regulator station in Oneonta... the replacement increases capacity by approximately 590 mcfh or 38% above existing capacity.' Solving for existing capacity: 590 / 0.38 = ~1,552.6 Mcf/h = ~37.3 MMcf/day = ~13.6 Bcf/year = ~0.385 Bcm/y — roughly 3.8x LOWER than the sheet's current 1.45 bcm/y. Candidate replacement value: Capacity ~0.385 bcm/y (CapacityUnits unchanged). Tier=medium/single-origin: this is one NYSEG capital-planning disclosure, quoted within one discovery response, and no second independent source with an explicit capacity figure was found (actual annual citygate delivery volumes for DeRuyter, also in this docket — e.g. ~2.25 million Dth in 2019 — were deliberately NOT used as a capacity comparator, since actual seasonal throughput is naturally far below rated/design capacity and is not a valid substitute for a capacity spec). Caveat: the 590-mcfh/38% figure describes capacity needed to supply a specific downstream regulator station (Winney Hill in Oneonta) via the pipe, which is a reasonable proxy for the line's throughput capacity but carries some interpretive uncertainty about whether it represents whole-system rated capacity. Recommend a human follow-up rather than an automatic overwrite given the single-origin, single-document derivation.
